label: Yehoshua (Joshua) — Part 3 — Chapters 16–24
summary_plain: The remaining tribal territories are assigned — Efrayim, Menasheh, Binyamin, Shim'on, Zevulun, Yissakhar, Asher, Naftali, Dan. The Levitical cities and cities of refuge are designated. Yehoshua's farewell speech: choose this day whom you will serve. As for me and my house, we will serve YHWH. The people renew the covenant at Shekhem. Yehoshua dies at 110 years old. Yosef's bones, which Moshe carried out of Egypt, are buried at Shekhem.
summary_scholarly: The covenant renewal at Shekhem (ch 24) is the climactic moment of the book — the people choose YHWH and commit to the covenant terms. The burial of Yosef's bones at Shekhem (24:32) fulfills the oath from Bereshit 50:25. The cycle is complete: Yosef was taken from the land to Egypt, and his bones return. The covenant people have entered the promised land, divided it, and renewed their commitment to YHWH.

key_terms.definition: Six cities designated in Yehoshua 20 where someone who kills unintentionally may flee to escape the blood-avenger. The accidental killer lives in the city until the death of the high priest. After that, they may return home safely. The cities are spread throughout the land — three on each side of the Jordan — to be accessible to all.

Forty-eight cities assigned to the tribe of Levi in chapter 21, taken from the territories of the other tribes. The Levites had no tribal land allotment; instead they received cities with pasture lands surrounding them. This distributed covenant servants throughout all twelve tribal territories.

In Yehoshua 22, after the tribes of Reuven, Gad, and half of Menasheh return across the Jordan, they build a large altar at the river. The western tribes mobilize for war, thinking it is unauthorized worship. The eastern tribes explain the altar is a witness — not for sacrifices, but to maintain their bond with the western tribes across the river.

The final event of Yehoshua (chapter 24): Yehoshua gathers all Yisra'el at Shekhem and presents YHWH's covenant history from Avraham forward. He challenges the people to choose whom they will serve. The people renew their covenant loyalty to YHWH. Yehoshua writes the terms in the scroll of YHWH's Torah and sets up a stone as witness.

Yehoshua's declaration in ch.24: 'Now therefore fear YHWH and serve him in sincerity and faithfulness... but as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH.' This is a personal covenant declaration made publicly — Yehoshua committing himself and his household before the entire assembly as a model for each family to decide.

After the covenant renewal in Yehoshua 24, Yehoshua sets up a large stone under the oak at Shekhem and declares: 'This stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of YHWH which he spoke to us.' Physical covenant markers are a consistent pattern — stones that witness the people's pledge.

The son of Aharon and high priest during Yehoshua's era, who worked alongside Yehoshua in the tribal allotment process. Eleazar's death is recorded at the close of the book (ch.24), alongside Yehoshua's burial and the burial of Yosef's bones at Shekhem.

Yehoshua 24:32 records the burial of Yosef's bones at Shekhem, in the field that Ya'akov had purchased. Yosef had commanded before his death in Mitzrayim: 'YHWH will surely take care of you — carry my bones up from here.' The burial at Shekhem fulfills Yosef's dying request and closes a 400-year covenant arc from Mitzrayim to the land.

key_terms.term: 'Choose this day whom you will serve'
key_terms.definition: Yehoshua's challenge to the assembly at Shekhem (ch.24): serve YHWH or serve the deities your ancestors served beyond the river or the Amorite deities of the land. The choice is presented as genuine, not coerced — but Yehoshua makes his own choice explicit. The people's declaration of loyalty is then written into the Torah scroll.

The city Yehoshua receives as his own inheritance (ch.19) in the hill country of Efrayim. He built the city and lived there. At his death (age 110), he was buried there. The book records Yehoshua's death and burial symmetrically with Kalev's: both faithful spies lived long, received personal inheritances, and died in the land they had believed YHWH would give.

faq.question: What was the purpose of the Trans-Jordan altar controversy?
faq.answer: The two and a half eastern tribes (Reuven, Gad, half-Menasheh) built a large altar at the Jordan when they returned to their territory. The western tribes nearly went to war over it, believing it was unauthorized worship — a violation of the central altar command. The eastern tribes clarified: the altar was not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but a visible witness that they were part of YHWH's covenant community despite the Jordan separating them from the Tabernacle. The crisis is resolved peacefully, confirming that covenant unity across geographic barriers requires visible symbols of belonging. The altar is named 'Witness' — not for worship, but for identity.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yosef's bones being buried at Shekhem?
faq.answer: Yosef made his brothers swear before he died in Mitzrayim that they would carry his bones up when YHWH brought them out. That oath was kept — the bones traveled through the wilderness for 40 years and through Yehoshua's entire conquest. Their burial at Shekhem (the field Ya'akov purchased, Bereshit 33:19) closes a 400-year covenant promise. Shekhem also has covenant resonance as the place where Avraham first arrived in Kena'an and YHWH first said 'to your descendants I will give this land.' The bones of Yosef buried there mark the land as the promised inheritance, now received.

faq.question: How does the Shekhem covenant renewal differ from earlier covenant ceremonies?
faq.answer: The Shekhem covenant renewal in ch.24 is unique in presenting the covenant as a genuine choice. Yehoshua reviews YHWH's history from Terah and Avraham forward, then says explicitly: 'Choose this day whom you will serve.' He even challenges the people's sincerity: 'You are not able to serve YHWH, for he is a holy Creator.' The people insist on their commitment three times. When they do, Yehoshua writes the terms in the Torah scroll and sets up a stone witness. This is covenant renewal as full public deliberation — not a forced loyalty declaration, but a witnessed, written, permanent commitment renewed by a generation that had lived through the conquest.

faq.question: Why did the death of the high priest release someone from a City of Refuge?
faq.answer: The high priest held a unique intercessory role — his life functioned as an atoning presence for the entire covenant community. The Orit tradition tied the accidental killer's status to the high priest's life: when the high priest died, something shifted in the covenant accounting for that period's unintentional bloodshed. The death of the high priest functioned like a communal atonement event, releasing those whose deaths were accidental from the legal jeopardy they carried. This is a covenant-law principle: the high priest's death has ransom power for those whose guilt was unintentional. It is not arbitrary timing but a deliberate theological structure.

faq.question: What does 'choose this day whom you will serve' mean for the covenant?
faq.answer: Yehoshua's challenge at Shekhem makes explicit what the covenant always assumed: loyalty to YHWH is a free decision, not an inherited compulsion. The ancestors had served deities beyond the river; the Amorites served their own deities. The land was full of competing covenant claims. Yehoshua requires the people to name their allegiance publicly, in the present moment — 'this day,' not in principle or theoretically. The challenge has teeth: Yehoshua warns them that YHWH is a holy and jealous Creator who will not forgive their turning away. The people choose, and Yehoshua writes it down — making it legally binding testimony that the entire assembly agreed.

faq.question: What is the significance of the witness stone at Shekhem?
faq.answer: The stone under the oak at Shekhem heard all the words of YHWH spoken at the covenant renewal. Yehoshua declares it will be a witness against the people if they lie about what they committed to. This continues a pattern across the Torah and former prophets of physical objects holding covenant testimony: the stone at Beit-El, the heap of stones at the Jordan crossing, the altar at the Trans-Jordan. Stones do not forget, cannot be bribed, and outlast the generation that placed them. The stone witness practice reflects a view of creation as participant in covenant — the land itself records the people's choices.

faq.question: Why did the Levites receive 48 cities rather than a territory?
faq.answer: The Levites' role was to serve YHWH at the central sanctuary and to teach Torah throughout Yisra'el — not to farm a tribal territory. If the Levites had their own land, they would be a thirteenth tribe with political and military interests. Instead, YHWH is their inheritance. By distributing 48 Levitical cities across all twelve tribal territories, the design ensures that covenant instruction was never more than a few hours' travel from any community in Yisra'el. The Cities of Refuge were also Levitical cities — the priests and teachers lived in the same cities that protected the accidentally guilty, connecting covenant law and covenant instruction in one location.

faq.question: How does Yehoshua close as a book?
faq.answer: The book closes with four deaths and burials: Yehoshua at 110 in Timnath-Serah; Eleazar the high priest in Gibeah; and Yosef's bones at Shekhem. The generation that saw YHWH's great works for Yisra'el is now gone. The book's final note — 'Yisra'el served YHWH all the days of Yehoshua and all the days of the elders who outlived Yehoshua' — is both a tribute and a warning. The covenant fidelity is tied to the living memory of the generation who saw it. Shofetim will immediately establish what happens when that generation is gone and the next generation does not know YHWH.

faq.question: What is the connection between the Cities of Refuge and the covenant calendar?
faq.answer: The six Cities of Refuge — Qedesh, Shekhem, Hevron on the west; Betzer, Ramoth, Golan on the east — are all Levitical cities. Their designation is tied directly to the covenant legal structure established at Sinai (Bamidbar 35). The accidental killer's situation involves covenant blood-guilt — a reality that affects the land itself in Orit theology. YHWH commands: 'You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land.' The Cities of Refuge are covenant infrastructure for maintaining the land's purity. Their distribution across all territories reflects the covenant's geographic comprehensiveness — no part of the land is beyond its reach.

faq.question: Why does Yehoshua warn the people they cannot serve YHWH?
faq.answer: Yehoshua's warning — 'You are not able to serve YHWH, for he is a holy Creator; he is a jealous Creator; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins' — is not pessimism but covenant realism. YHWH's standard is total loyalty. The people have been surrounded by other deities in Kena'an; they carry ancestral memories of Mitzrayim's gods; they are not naturally equipped for exclusive covenant fidelity. Yehoshua's warning aims to make the commitment serious: if you say 'we will serve YHWH' and then turn away, you have made a witnessed, written oath against yourself. The commitment must be informed and sober, not enthusiastic and shallow. The people insist anyway — which is exactly what Yehoshua wants.
